identification.summary: Financially motivated cybercrime group that Microsoft says develops, distributes and manages many payloads, including Trickbot, BazaLoader and AnchorDNS [S1][S2]. It ran the Ryuk ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) program until Ryuk shut down in June 2021, then ran its successor Conti, and is also linked to Diavol [S1][S2]. In 2022 Microsoft called DEV-0193 "the most prolific ransomware-associated cybercriminal activity group active today" [S1]. MITRE describes the overlapping Wizard Spider group as Russia-based and financially motivated. Wizard Spider has created and deployed TrickBot since at least 2016 and has run ransomware campaigns against organizations from major corporations to hospitals [S9].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: tracked since October 2020 [S1][S2]. MITRE (Wizard Spider): TrickBot creation and deployment since at least 2016 [S9]. Microsoft: Trickbot discovered in 2016 [S5]. Mandiant: Ryuk deployed after TrickBot infections (TEMP.MixMaster) since at least December 2017 [S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Periwinkle Tempest, formerly DEV-0193; the Security Insider profile lists the alias 'Trickbot LLC' [S2]. Microsoft's naming map gives origin 'Russia' and other names DEV-0193 and WIZARD SPIDER, but it also maps WIZARD SPIDER to the separate group Storm-0230 ('Conti Team 1') [S10]. 'Tempest' marks financially motivated actors in Microsoft's taxonomy [S11]. Cluster boundaries matter. Microsoft separates the payload developer and RaaS operator (Periwinkle Tempest / DEV-0193) from affiliates that deployed its ransomware: Pistachio Tempest (DEV-0237), which Microsoft lists as also known as FIN12, and DEV-0230 [S1][S12]. MITRE's Wizard Spider (G0102) merges all of these: its aliases include Periwinkle Tempest, DEV-0193, Pistachio Tempest, DEV-0237, FIN12, UNC1878, TEMP.MixMaster, Grim Spider, GOLD BLACKBURN and ITG23 [S9]. Facts sourced to Mandiant's FIN12, UNC1878 or TEMP.MixMaster reporting describe ransomware-deployment clusters that use Trickbot/BazarLoader access. They are not necessarily Periwinkle Tempest itself [S6][S7][S8].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor identified in cited sources. Financially motivated cybercrime enterprise [S2][S9]. Microsoft's naming map lists origin as Russia [S10]. MITRE describes Wizard Spider as Russia-based [S9]. In 2019 Mandiant assessed the TrickBot administrator group as suspected to be based in Eastern Europe [S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft tracks Periwinkle Tempest as a named, financially motivated actor and lists its origin as Russia [S2][S10]. The sources gathered give no stated confidence level. In 2019 Mandiant said it had found no evidence for reports attributing Ryuk to North Korea. Mandiant said Hermes code similarities were insufficient for that attribution because the Hermes kit was sold underground [S6]. No government attribution document was retrieved for this record.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and actor tracking since October 2020 [S1][S2]. Leaked Conti chats from February 2022 confirmed the scale of DEV-0193 activity [S1]. Infrastructure overlaps seen during CVE-2021-40444 exploitation [S3]. MITRE ATT&CK group profile [S9].

objectives: Financial gain [S2][S11]. The group earns money by developing and running malware and RaaS platforms (Trickbot, BazaLoader, AnchorDNS, Ryuk, Conti, Diavol) that give network access to ransomware affiliates [S1][S2]. Microsoft says Trickbot evolved from a banking trojan into an access-as-a-service backdoor for other malware such as Ryuk [S5].

sectors: Financial services, government and other verticals (Trickbot distribution, 2020) [S4]
Government, financial services, manufacturing, service providers, high-tech (TrickBot phishing preceding Ryuk, 2018) [S6]
Hospitals, retirement communities and medical centers (UNC1878 Ryuk campaigns, 2020) [S7]
regions: Global: Trickbot seen in large and small enterprises around the world [S4]
United States: primary recipient of the 2018 TrickBot campaign that led to Ryuk deployments [S6]
North America: about 85 percent of known FIN12 (affiliate) victims [S8]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's profile lists education and healthcare as targeted industries and does not name regions [S2]. As a payload developer, Periwinkle Tempest reaches broad victim sets through mass Trickbot/BazaLoader distribution. Affiliates then pick high-value victims for ransomware [S1][S4]. Victims of the FIN12 affiliate mostly had more than $300 million in revenue, and almost 20 percent were in healthcare. These figures describe FIN12 (Microsoft's Pistachio Tempest), not Periwinkle Tempest directly [S8][S12].

capabilities.summary: Develops and runs modular malware and loaders: Trickbot, BazaLoader (Mandiant's KEGTAP/SINGLEMALT/WINEKEY family) and AnchorDNS. Also runs ransomware programs: Ryuk until June 2021, then Conti and Diavol [S1][S2][S7]. Hired developers from Emotet, Qakbot and IcedID [S1]. Trickbot added plug-ins, access-as-a-service backdoors and mining features. It used compromised MikroTik routers as C2 proxies on non-standard ports, gaining access through default passwords, brute force or CVE-2018-14847 [S5]. Microsoft notes a subgroup, DEV-0365, that provides Cobalt Strike Beacon as a service [S1]. DEV-0193 infrastructure was involved in attacks that exploited CVE-2021-40444, and some of that infrastructure also delivered BazaLoader and Trickbot payloads [S1][S3]. Phishing lures used current events (COVID-19, shipping, Black Lives Matter), invoices, complaints and financial themes [S4]. BazarLoader-linked campaigns linked to actor-controlled Google Docs and could lead to ransomware within about 24 hours of initial compromise [S7]. MITRE maps the merged Wizard Spider group to a broad toolset that includes Cobalt Strike, Mimikatz, BloodHound, AdFind and Rubeus [S9].

campaigns.name: Trickbot emergence
campaigns.summary: Trickbot discovered; later evolved with plug-ins and access-as-a-service backdoors for ransomware such as Ryuk. MITRE says Wizard Spider has created and deployed TrickBot since at least 2016.

campaigns.name: TrickBot-to-Ryuk operations (TEMP.MixMaster)
campaigns.summary: Mandiant tracks interactive Ryuk deployment after TrickBot infections from at least December 2017, rising in late 2018. The campaign reached mainly US organizations and reportedly made about $3.7M in BTC. Mandiant could not confirm that one operator ran the whole chain.

campaigns.name: Microsoft-led Trickbot disruption
campaigns.summary: Microsoft worked with telecom providers worldwide to disrupt key Trickbot infrastructure, citing Trickbot's role as an entry point for Ryuk.

campaigns.name: BazarLoader/Ryuk campaigns against healthcare (UNC1878)
campaigns.summary: Mandiant reports KEGTAP/SINGLEMALT/WINEKEY (BazarLoader) campaigns leading to Cobalt Strike and Ryuk deployment against hospitals, retirement communities and medical centers. Mandiant attributes most of this to UNC1878, which Microsoft says overlaps DEV-0193 activity.

campaigns.name: Ryuk RaaS shutdown; transition to Conti
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says DEV-0193 managed Ryuk until its June 2021 shutdown, followed by its successor Conti and by Diavol.

campaigns.name: CVE-2021-40444 exploitation overlap
campaigns.summary: Some infrastructure that hosted CVE-2021-40444 exploit content also delivered BazaLoader and Trickbot payloads, overlapping DEV-0193.

campaigns.name: Conti chat leaks
campaigns.summary: Leaked Conti chats confirmed the scale of DEV-0193 activity.

campaigns.name: Trickbot MikroTik C2 infrastructure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft exposed Trickbot's use of compromised MikroTik routers as C2 proxies.

campaigns.name: Last observed Conti deployment (Microsoft data)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft had not seen a Conti deployment in its data since 19 April 2022, as affiliates moved to other payloads.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated cybercrime enterprise (Trickbot LLC) that Microsoft lists with Russia origin. It recruits developers from other malware operations (Emotet, Qakbot, IcedID) [S1][S2][S10].
diamond.capability: Trickbot, BazaLoader, AnchorDNS loaders and backdoors; Ryuk, Conti and Diavol ransomware sold as RaaS; Cobalt Strike Beacon provided as a service via DEV-0365 [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Botnet C2 proxied through compromised MikroTik routers on ports such as 443 and 449 [S5]. Payload-delivery infrastructure shared with CVE-2021-40444 exploitation [S3]. Actor-controlled Google Docs links in phishing [S7].
diamond.victim: Broad enterprise victim pool reached through mass Trickbot distribution. Microsoft-listed industries are education and healthcare; hospitals and medical centers were hit by affiliate ransomware [S2][S4][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit-driven ransomware economy in which developers and RaaS operators rent access and payloads to affiliates such as Pistachio Tempest (DEV-0237) and DEV-0230 [S1][S12].
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise networks reached by email phishing. Office/MSHTML exploit (CVE-2021-40444). Exposed or vulnerable IoT routers (MikroTik RouterOS CVE-2018-14847) used as relays [S3][S4][S5].

gaps: No government attribution or sanctions document (e.g., US/UK Trickbot-related sanctions or DOJ indictments) was retrieved; government sites and press were unreachable, so no official naming of individuals is included.
Microsoft gives no stated confidence level for the Russia origin in the sources gathered; the Security Insider profile does not state origin or targeted regions [S2][S10].

Cluster boundaries: MITRE G0102 merges Periwinkle Tempest with Pistachio Tempest/DEV-0237/FIN12, UNC1878 and others [S9], while Microsoft tracks Periwinkle Tempest, Pistachio Tempest and Storm-0230 (WIZARD SPIDER, Conti Team 1) separately [S10]. Which intrusions belong to the developer versus affiliates is not resolved in open sources gathered.

CrowdStrike (Wizard Spider/Grim Spider), Secureworks (GOLD BLACKBURN/GOLD ULRICK), IBM X-Force (ITG23), PRODAFT, Cybereason (Anchor), SentinelOne (PowerTrick) and EuRepoC reports in the imported references could not be opened (hosts unreachable); their content is not used here.
CISA/FBI/HHS joint advisory AA20-302A on ransomware targeting healthcare (October 2020) could not be opened.

Activity after the 2022 Conti wind-down is not described in Microsoft's January 2024 profile beyond historical payloads; current operations, successor brands and status after law-enforcement actions are unverified.
Aliases GOLD ULRICK, UNC2053 and Trickbot LLC vendor mappings in the imported record were not verified against primary vendor pages, except 'Trickbot LLC', which Microsoft lists [S2].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is enterprise email gateways and user endpoints that receive commodity phishing. Edge routers (MikroTik) can be co-opted as C2 relays, so friendly or contractor network devices may become adversary infrastructure [S4][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): Trickbot/BazaLoader footholds are sold or handed to ransomware affiliates. Mandiant reports ransomware sometimes within 24 hours of initial compromise and an average FIN12 time-to-ransom of 2.5 days in 1H 2021. Hospitals and medical centers have been hit, so mission impacts on medical support and base services can be severe [S7][S8]. STEP 3 (adversary template): phishing with current-event, invoice or Google Docs lures, then Trickbot/BazaLoader, then Cobalt Strike Beacon, then domain discovery and credential theft, then PsExec-style Ryuk/Conti deployment against domain controllers and critical servers [S4][S6][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic mass loader distribution, with access monetized by affiliates through ransomware against high-revenue, healthcare and education targets [S1][S2][S8]. MDCOA is coordinated ransomware against healthcare or base-support providers during a crisis, as seen in the 2020 healthcare campaigns [S7]. Candidate indicators: Trickbot/BazaLoader detections, anomalous BITS jobs or Run-key persistence, Cobalt Strike beacons, traffic to routers on ports 443/449 with unusual NAT redirection, and exploitation of Office/MSHTML flaws such as CVE-2021-40444 [S3][S5][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat any Trickbot or BazaLoader detection on DODIN-connected or mission-partner systems as a likely early sign of ransomware. Escalate on a timeline measured in hours, not days [S7]. (2) Authorities: this is a criminal actor. Disruption precedent is a Microsoft-led civil and technical action with telecom providers [S4], so responses rely on law-enforcement and private-sector partners. Do not treat this as a state-sponsored threat without government attribution. (3) Mission assurance: healthcare, education and service-provider dependencies (medical treatment facilities, contractors) are documented victim sets. Validate offline backups and segmentation for domain controllers, the hosts ransomware operators targeted [S2][S6][S7]. (4) Coordination: affiliates (Pistachio Tempest/FIN12, DEV-0230) may carry out the final ransomware stage, so share indicators across vendor naming schemes and avoid single-name attribution in reporting [S1][S12].
